articles.title: An update on independent evaluators
articles.preview: Anthropic has embedded a team from the nonprofit METR inside the company with access comparable to its own risk staff. METR may publish its findings on Anthropic's risks without the company being able to block them.

summary.t: Anthropic recently pledged stronger independent checks of its models and signed a White House accord on superintelligence. As a first concrete step, six METR staff now work with company laptops, desks and internal tools, roughly on par with Anthropic's own risk teams. Employees are encouraged to talk to them like colleagues, except about customer data, legal advice and model architecture.

METR can publish its assessment of Anthropic's risk levels and incidents, and Anthropic cannot veto it. The company may only demand redactions in narrow, predefined areas, and METR is free to say publicly whether it thinks those redactions were justified. Anthropic compares the setup to bank supervisors who sit inside large banks.

Anthropic is building a tiered model: narrow, approved studies at the first level, independent publication at the second and full embedding like METR's at the third. SecureBio is currently reviewing the chemical and biological weapons chapter of a risk report, while work with Accenture, Faculty and possibly Hugging Face is at an earlier stage. The company says every frontier AI lab should open up in the same way.

articles.title: Preparing for the 2026 US midterms
articles.preview: Ahead of the US midterms, Anthropic is building official voting information and live election results into Claude. It also reports how often people use Claude for politics and where its safeguards still have gaps.

summary.h: How Americans use Claude for politics
summary.t: Anthropic analysed a quarter of a million US conversations from one week. Roughly one in seventeen touched on politics, policy or social issues, and about half a percent were about elections or voting. Almost nobody asked Claude whom to vote for; people were more interested in where candidates stand on issues. Requests that broke the election rules were extremely rare.

Claude already shows a banner linking to the nonpartisan TurboVote service when people ask about registration or polling places. Later this month it will start answering such questions with state-specific official information from Democracy Works. On election night and in the following days it will show the latest official results.

Anthropic says its newest models score 99 percent on its internal test for political evenhandedness and refuse fewer political questions than before. Three outside groups also tested Claude. They found it engaged seriously with contested topics but sometimes added unrequested counterarguments, and one group found an older model softened right-leaning arguments more often. Anthropic says it is adjusting short yes-or-no answers and how it adds caveats so that all sides are treated alike.

Two independent institutes probed Claude's defences in the US, Israel and Brazil, all of which hold major elections this year. A single harmful request was reliably refused, but a campaign split into many harmless-looking steps could slip through. Anthropic has since added detection for such multi-step abuse, for fake news sites and accounts, and for foreign state actors. It also cites recent cases it shut down, including a foreign-run fake news site pushing Russian, Iranian and North Korean narratives and schemes that churned out fake election news for ad revenue.

articles.title: Anthropic opens Singapore office and signs MOU with the Government of Singapore
articles.preview: Anthropic has opened an office in Singapore, its fifth in the Asia-Pacific region, and signed a cooperation agreement with the country's digital ministry. Singapore is among the heaviest users of Claude relative to its population.

summary.t: The memorandum covers cooperation on AI safety, security and model testing, research on AI adoption, and responsible use in the public and private sectors. Anthropic plans technical exchanges with Singapore's safety institutions, support for small businesses and AI training for civil servants. It will also share research data and policy advice as the country writes its AI rules.

According to Anthropic's own index, Singapore ranks second out of 121 countries for Claude use per head. More than 1,500 engineers at the government's technology agency use Claude Code, and the bank DBS and the sovereign wealth fund GIC are rolling it out internally. Grab says a Claude-based sales assistant saves its teams about 40,000 hours per quarter, and Sea uses it for Shopee's customer service. Regulated firms can now run Claude within the region through Amazon Bedrock.

articles.title: Bank of America hired 1,000 contractors to patch software flaws exposed by Anthropic's Mythos
articles.preview: Bank of America hired 1,000 extra contractors to patch software flaws that powerful AI models such as Anthropic's Mythos can uncover. The bank spent a few hundred million dollars on the clean-up and related compliance issues last quarter.

summary.t: CEO Brian Moynihan said the bank reacted quickly once frontier models like Mythos appeared, because they can find and exploit decades-old code weaknesses. The contractors joined about 3,000 in-house staff working on the problem and are still there. It is one of the first times a major US company has put numbers on what Mythos-era security costs.

Moynihan expects patching costs to fall once the backlog is cleared, even as the stock dropped up to 8 percent on the day. At the same time, around 130 internal AI projects are expected to save $700 million in 2027, up from $300 million this year.

articles.title: CoreWeave credit default swaps hit distress levels as investors sour on AI debt
articles.preview: Investors are losing patience with CoreWeave's heavy borrowing: its bond yields have climbed above 15 percent and the cost of insuring its debt against default has hit distress levels. The stock and other neocloud names fell further.

summary.h: Warning signs in the bond market
summary.t: CoreWeave has taken on more than $51 billion in debt and obligations to build AI data centers. The price of its credit default swaps jumped by a third in a week, a level analysts read as financial distress. Traders say the market is no longer willing to fund AI debt that is not backed by operating cash flow.

summary.h: Demand is real, cash is not yet
summary.t: Nobody doubts the demand, since CoreWeave has contracts with all the big cloud providers and a backlog of more than $100 billion. The worry is that its free cash flow is deeply negative. The CEO called the sell-off irrational, but analysts warn that fears like these can become self-fulfilling and spread, and Oracle's default insurance also rose this week.

articles.title: Traders pile into 'bubble puts' on CoreWeave as neocloud stocks plunge
articles.preview: Shares of neocloud companies that rent out AI chips plunged after CoreWeave's bond yields hit new highs, and CoreWeave lost 15 percent in a day. Options traders placed large bets on further falls.

summary.t: Trading in CoreWeave options rose to more than seven times the usual volume, with puts clearly outnumbering calls. One investor bought puts worth about $1.9 million that only pay off if the stock falls another 42 percent by mid-December. A trading coach called them bubble insurance, probably a hedge against a broader slide in AI stocks.

articles.title: Apple and Meta team up to make Muse AI model run on Mac computers
articles.preview: Former rivals Apple and Meta are working together: Meta's new open-weight AI model Muse Spark Open now runs directly on linked Mac Studio computers. The move reflects how the AI race is reshaping old alliances in Silicon Valley.

summary.h: A big model on the desk
summary.t: Muse Spark Open is a very large open-weight model that developers can download and run on their own hardware. Linking two to four Mac Studios is enough to use it for coding, video analysis and agent tasks without the cloud, which saves money and keeps data local. Apple tuned its MLX software so the model can be split across several machines. The catch is price: a suitable Mac Studio with the top M5 Ultra chip costs at least $10,799.

Apple and Meta had avoided public deals for years, and Apple's 2021 privacy changes cost Meta billions in ad revenue. Under Apple's new CEO John Ternus the tone has changed, and Zuckerberg and Ternus publicly praised each other. Meta's AI chief credits a former Apple manager on his team with making the deal happen.

For Meta, the release shows its rebooted AI effort is gaining ground, though it is not its strongest model. For Apple, it is a showcase for its own AI chips in a market dominated by Nvidia, at a time when its new Siri still trails leading chatbots. Apple also works with Google's Gemini, and its earlier ChatGPT tie-up with OpenAI has since soured into a lawsuit.

articles.title: AWS, Anthropic race to deploy army of specialized engineers key to proving AI spending will pay off
articles.preview: After pouring billions into AI, Amazon, OpenAI, Anthropic and Google are now racing to train specialised engineers who put the technology to work inside companies. Investors increasingly want proof that the spending pays off.

summary.h: The new key job in AI
summary.t: So-called forward deployed engineers combine AI and software skills with an understanding of how businesses run, and they work directly with customers to turn experiments into usable systems. US job ads for the role rose from fewer than 200 in 2023 to more than 7,300 in the first nine months of this year. Median advertised pay is now around $195,000, three times the national median, and consulting firms like Deloitte and Accenture are among the biggest recruiters.

AWS is investing $1 billion in its own team of such engineers, starting with several hundred. OpenAI has a deployment business backed by more than $4 billion and is buying a consulting firm to add about 150 specialists. Anthropic is spending $100 million to train 10,000 engineers from its customers and partners by the end of 2027, in a residency modelled on how doctors are trained. Accenture and Google Cloud are retraining experienced developers into a 1,000-person team.

Industry insiders say technical skills can be taught, but judgement in messy customer projects takes experience. Early case studies report faster engineering work and freed-up capacity, but not independently verified financial returns. Anthropic admits it is too early to measure the results of its programme.

articles.title: Memory stocks are getting hammered. China and a 2029 oversupply are the big worries
articles.preview: Memory chip stocks have slumped this week: SK Hynix lost 26 percent in five days, Samsung 22 percent and Micron about 11 percent. Investors fear Chinese competition and a possible glut of memory chips from 2029.

summary.t: The sell-off began when Chinese chipmaker CXMT announced a server memory product with a new, denser design. Several analysts doubt it can produce such chips in volume with good yields. A South Korean newspaper column added to the jitters by warning that a flood of new supply could hit in 2029 and end the boom, a point Elon Musk echoed.

summary.h: Is the old boom-and-bust cycle over?
summary.t: AI data centers have made memory a key component and driven prices to record highs. New factories take three to five years, so many analysts expect the shortage to last until 2028. Counterpoint Research forecasts a price drop of about 23 percent in 2028, but notes that long-term supply contracts with price floors should prevent the steep crashes of the past.

articles.title: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang urges U.S.-China dialogue on 'potentially dangerous' AI
articles.preview: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang says the US must talk to Chinese AI companies about the risks of the 'potentially dangerous' technology. He suggests Britain could host such talks.

summary.t: Unlike the heads of OpenAI and Anthropic, Huang opposes tighter regulation and instead calls for more exchange between researchers. Washington and Beijing have discussed an AI channel for serious incidents, and Xi Jinping recently said both countries could cooperate to prevent AI misuse.

articles.title: TSMC posts record profit for a sixth straight quarter, beating estimates on AI boom
articles.preview: TSMC has reported a record profit for the sixth quarter in a row, with net income up almost 69 percent on the year. The world's largest contract chipmaker says demand for AI chips still exceeds its capacity.

summary.t: An operating margin of almost 59 percent shows how much pricing power TSMC has. For the fourth quarter it expects revenue to rise another 14 percent, and it plans to invest significantly more from 2026 to 2028 than in the previous three years. Chips at 3 nanometres made up the largest share of sales, and high-performance computing accounted for about two thirds of revenue.

TSMC checks whether customers can actually finance and deploy the chips they order, and says demand remains well above supply even after those checks. Its second Arizona plant is built and should start mass production in 2027, slightly ahead of plan, and the company is reportedly considering Texas as well.

articles.title: Anthropic's third-quarter revenue is said to hit $16.8 billion ahead of IPO
articles.preview: Anthropic told investors its third-quarter revenue reached $16.8 billion, up from $11.6 billion in the second quarter, ahead of an IPO reportedly planned for November. The company also said it was profitable on an adjusted basis and cash-flow positive.

articles.title: Nvidia, AMD, Dell sell-off in global tech rout on AI funding worries
articles.preview: The global sell-off in AI and chip stocks continued: the 20 most valuable AI and semiconductor companies have lost more than $1 trillion in market value this week. Rising interest rates, financing worries and fiercer competition weighed on sentiment.

summary.t: Nvidia, AMD and Intel slipped, Dell fell 9 percent, and in Asia SK Hynix, Samsung, SoftBank and Advantest dropped sharply. In Europe, Infineon and ASM International lost ground too. Neocloud stocks recovered somewhat after Nvidia's CEO said CoreWeave's cost of capital was actually falling.

Hot US inflation data has raised the prospect of further rate hikes, which makes the debt-funded AI build-out more expensive, and the heads of Broadcom and Intel have warned that financing could become the main bottleneck. Fears of a memory chip glut and new Chinese competition added pressure. Analyst Dan Ives calls it a financing problem rather than a demand problem and sees a buying opportunity unless big cloud providers cut spending or chip rental prices fall.

articles.title: OpenAI sued by 8 states over ChatGPT safety concerns
articles.preview: Eight US states, including Iowa, Kansas and Arizona, have sued OpenAI, arguing that ChatGPT is an unsafe product that harms children and misleads parents. OpenAI points to its age-specific safeguards.

summary.t: Iowa's attorney general says ChatGPT gives dangerous medical advice, encourages harm and coaches people toward suicide while posing as a friend. Florida had already sued in June, and several wrongful death cases blame the chatbot for fuelling harmful delusions.

The company says it has protections many rivals lack, including parental controls, break reminders and ChatGPT for Teens, and that it wants industry-wide rules. It concedes that no system is perfect and promises further safeguards.

articles.title: Dell stock plunges 11%, leading data center sell-off as fears mount about 'enterprise AI timing'
articles.preview: Dell shares fell 11 percent and pulled other data center suppliers such as HPE, Oracle and Super Micro down with them. Barclays doubts that companies are actually spending enough on AI to justify the hardware boom.

summary.h: A downgrade after a huge run
summary.t: Dell had more than quadrupled this year, and HPE and NetApp also rose strongly before Barclays cut all three to hold. The analysts argue that higher revenues mainly reflect expensive memory being passed on to customers, not a wave of enterprise AI purchases. Companies typically spend only about 5 percent of their IT budgets on AI, and only a quarter of that goes on hardware.

articles.title: OpenAI’s Sachin Katti to leave infrastructure role, stay on as advisor
articles.preview: Sachin Katti, head of infrastructure at OpenAI, is leaving after about a year to build something new but will stay on as an adviser. His deputy, a former xAI infrastructure chief, takes over the compute organisation.

summary.t: The compute team plans the data centers OpenAI needs to train and run its models, and the company aims to spend around $600 billion on computing by 2030. The change comes as local opposition to data centers grows and has become an issue in the midterm elections. It is the latest in a series of senior departures this year, which OpenAI's president describes as normal for a young company.

articles.title: CoreWeave shares tumble as bond yields near 15% on concern about AI borrowing binge
articles.preview: CoreWeave's shares dropped 15.5 percent in one day while yields on its bonds rose to almost 15 percent. Investors fear some tech firms are borrowing too heavily to build AI data centers.

summary.t: A Wells Fargo strategist says the period of cheap AI financing is fading and lenders now scrutinise every dollar. Analysts note CoreWeave spends almost like a hyperscaler without a hyperscaler's balance sheet, and S&P rates its debt as junk. The CEO insists its order backlog covers all obligations.
Alphabet, Amazon, Meta and Oracle have issued more than $228 billion in bonds this year, over twice the 2025 total. Oracle fell almost 9 percent, and smaller AI names suffered most.

articles.title: Tech giants race to get AI gadgets on shelves for holiday rush
articles.preview: Apple, Amazon and Microsoft are all launching AI gadgets for the holiday season, from an Nvidia-powered laptop to Alexa tablets and Apple's new HomeView hub. Whether consumers will pay extra for AI hardware is still uncertain.

summary.t: Microsoft started with a $2,599 Windows laptop built around an Nvidia AI chip that can run powerful models without the cloud. Amazon replaced its budget Fire line with pricier Alexa tablets, the largest at $550, which can read what is on screen and act on it. Apple followed with HomeView, a $299 smart home display with Siri AI and face recognition for each family member.

Consumer sentiment is at a 12-year low, and AI servers are absorbing so much memory that device prices have risen and smartphone and laptop shipments have fallen. Analysts expect modest sales at first; the goal is to get early adopters used to AI at home. Bain predicts record US holiday sales above $1 trillion, but says much of the growth is inflation and that electronics may stay flat.

Companies are also chasing recurring revenue: the new Alexa needs a monthly fee or Prime, and some HomeView features require a bigger iCloud plan. Ollama's CEO argues there is a real audience for owning AI on your own device instead of renting it. Apple's biggest test may be its $1,999 folding iPhone Duo arriving next week.

articles.title: ASML says it's getting order interest through 2030 as profit smashes expectations
articles.preview: ASML's third-quarter profit beat expectations, and some customers already want to place orders for 2029 and 2030. The Dutch chip equipment maker raised the lower end of its 2026 sales forecast.

summary.t: ASML is the only maker of the extreme ultraviolet machines used to produce the most advanced chips. Its CEO says planned supply for 2027 and 2028 will not fully cover customer demand, and the company is looking for ways to expand capacity beyond the 30 percent increase already planned. Samsung and TSMC have committed to its next-generation High NA machines, seen as key to future growth. China is expected to make up about a fifth of sales, despite export restrictions on the most advanced tools.

articles.title: Here's where Jim Cramer stands on this newly public AI infrastructure stock
articles.preview: Jim Cramer advises investors to keep their distance from Accelevation, a newly listed supplier of data center equipment. He prefers established names and expects political headwinds for data centers until after the midterms.

summary.h: A weak start and thin margins
summary.t: Accelevation, which installs power and cooling equipment in data centers, priced its IPO below the planned range and now trades around $15. Revenue has more than doubled, but higher labour costs and project problems have squeezed margins. Cramer would rather own GE Vernova and Eaton, and suggests waiting three weeks for the election before buying data center suppliers.

articles.title: Anthropic urges court in Washington, DC, to rehear appeal of Pentagon blacklisting
articles.preview: Anthropic has asked a federal appeals court in Washington to rehear its case against the Pentagon, which labelled the company a national security risk. Anthropic says the label is retaliation for refusing to allow mass surveillance and autonomous weapons.

summary.t: Anthropic signed a $200 million Pentagon contract in 2025, but talks about using Claude on the military's AI platform collapsed. In March the Defense Department declared the company a supply chain risk, barring contractors from using its models. A divided appeals panel upheld that decision in September, while a San Francisco judge ruled in a parallel case that it violated Anthropic's free speech rights.

articles.title: Der Börsen-Tag: Nasdaq mit knallrotem Start
articles.preview: Die Wall Street ist mit deutlichen Verlusten bei KI-Aktien gestartet, die Nasdaq-Indizes fielen um bis zu 1,2 Prozent. Nvidia, AMD, Micron und CoreWeave gaben spürbar nach, während Anleger in sichere Anleihen flüchteten.

articles.title: Der Börsen-Tag: "Blase geplatzt?" - Chip-Höhenrausch folgt der Kurskater
articles.preview: Nach monatelanger Rally hat der Philadelphia-Halbleiterindex 20 Prozent von seinem Hoch verloren, liegt auf Sicht von drei Jahren aber weit im Plus. Im Video ordnet ntv-Börsenexperte Frank Meyer ein, ob die Chip-Blase geplatzt ist.

articles.title: Der Börsen-Tag: Über 700 Milliarden Dollar vernichtet - Dilemma für Fed
articles.preview: Die hohe US-Inflation hat erst die Wall Street und dann die Börse in Südkorea ins Minus gezogen, Zins- und KI-Sorgen sind zurück. Im Video erklärt ntv-Börsenexpertin Nancy Lanzendörfer, ob eine US-Zinserhöhung früher kommt als gedacht.

articles.title: Der Börsen-Tag: DocMorris hebt erneut Prognose an
articles.preview: Die Online-Apotheke DocMorris hebt nach einem starken dritten Quartal ihre Jahresprognose erneut an und erwartet nun 12,5 bis 15 Prozent Umsatzwachstum. Das bereinigte operative Ergebnis war früher als geplant erstmals positiv, getrieben vom stark wachsenden Geschäft mit Rezeptmedikamenten.

articles.title: Der Börsen-Tag: Tiefrotes Tech-Aktien-Festival im vorbörslichen US-Handel
articles.preview: Positive Signale von Anthropic und TSMC zur KI-Nachfrage haben die Anleger vorbörslich nicht beruhigt. Intel, Nvidia, Micron, Marvell, Oracle und CoreWeave lagen erneut im Minus.

articles.title: Der Börsen-Tag: Mangel an KI-Aktien ist für Dax hilfreich
articles.preview: Der DAX hält sich im Tech-Ausverkauf erstaunlich gut, weil er kaum KI-Aktien enthält. Während Infineon und Siemens Energy verlieren, stützen defensive Werte wie die Deutsche Telekom und Pharmatitel.

articles.title: Viele Kurse fallen immer weiter: Ausverkauf von Tech-Aktien an US-Börsen vernichtet Billionenwerte
articles.preview: Der Ausverkauf bei Tech-Aktien setzt sich an den US-Börsen fort: Die Nasdaq fiel deutlich, und der Philadelphia-Halbleiterindex steuert nach sieben Verlusttagen auf mehr als zwei Billionen Dollar Wertverlust zu. Anleger zweifeln, ob sich die KI-Investitionen auszahlen.

summary.t: Neben hohen Bewertungen belastet die Aussicht auf weiter steigende Zinsen, die Kredite für den KI-Ausbau verteuern. Zusätzlich dämpfte TSMC mit vorsichtigen Tönen für 2027 die Stimmung, und CoreWeave brach zeitweise erneut ein. Ein Analyst bringt es so auf den Punkt: Hohe Nachfrage nach KI ist noch kein profitables Geschäftsmodell.

articles.title: Furcht vor einer Insolvenzwelle: Tech-Ausverkauf erfasst Europas Börsen
articles.preview: Der Tech-Ausverkauf aus den USA und Asien hat Europas Börsen erreicht: Infineon, Aixtron und Suss Microtec brachen um acht bis neun Prozent ein. Der DAX hielt sich dank weniger Chipwerten vergleichsweise gut.

summary.t: Auslöser war die unerwartet hohe US-Inflation, die die ohnehin angespannte Lage verschärfte; in Japan und Südkorea fielen die Leitindizes um 5 und 7,5 Prozent. Ein Portfoliomanager sieht darin die Angst vor einer großen Korrektur. Dass selbst starke Zahlen von TSMC verpufften, werten Experten als Warnsignal.

Die Kosten für eine Absicherung gegen einen Zahlungsausfall von Oracle, das mit über 120 Milliarden Dollar verschuldet ist, stiegen auf ein Rekordhoch. Etwas Entlastung kam von fallenden Anleiherenditen und einem leicht sinkenden Ölpreis.

articles.title: Deutlicher Gewinnsprung: Chip-Riese TSMC setzt Höhenflug fort
articles.preview: Der Chipfertiger TSMC hat zum sechsten Mal in Folge einen Rekordgewinn erzielt: Der Nettogewinn stieg um 69 Prozent auf umgerechnet rund 21 Milliarden Euro. Der Konzern arbeitet wegen des KI-Booms an der Kapazitätsgrenze.

summary.t: In diesem Jahr will TSMC umgerechnet 52 bis 56 Milliarden Euro in neue Fertigung stecken, mittelfristig 265 Milliarden Dollar allein in Arizona. Analysten halten selbst das für zu wenig, Insidern zufolge prüft der Konzern ein weiteres Werk in Texas.

articles.title: Sorge wegen hoher Inflation: Tech-Werte rutschen an der Wall Street ab
articles.preview: Überraschend hohe US-Inflation hat die Angst vor weiteren Zinserhöhungen geschürt und vor allem Tech- und KI-Werte belastet. Die Nasdaq verlor 1,9 Prozent, so viel wie seit Ende Juli nicht mehr.

summary.t: Die Inflationsrate stieg im September auf 3,7 Prozent, Händler sehen die Wahrscheinlichkeit einer Zinserhöhung noch in diesem Monat nun bei 37 Prozent. Oracle, CoreWeave und Nebius brachen ein, Dell und HPE rutschten nach einer Herabstufung durch Barclays deutlich ab. Der Halbleiterindex fiel den sechsten Tag in Folge.

articles.title: Firmensterben erwartet: Studie sieht Billionen-Abschreibungen im KI-Bereich
articles.preview: Laut einer Gartner-Studie werden sich die weltweiten Investitionen in KI-Rechenzentren vorerst nicht auszahlen: Bis 2030 drohen Abschreibungen auf Projekte im Wert von 3,5 Billionen Dollar. Viele kleinere Anbieter dürften verschwinden.

summary.t: Bis 2030 müssten Rechenzentrumsbetreiber laut Gartner rund 8,5 Billionen Dollar Umsatz erzielen, um ihre Investitionen zu rechtfertigen, die KI-Erlöse dürften aber höchstens 3,6 Billionen erreichen. Weil Server schnell veralten, rechne sich der Ausbau erst um 2032. Besonders gefährdet seien spezialisierte Neoclouds: 80 Prozent könnten schließen oder übernommen werden, während AWS, Google und Microsoft genug andere Einnahmen haben.

articles.title: Lange Haftstrafe droht: OpenAI-Mitarbeiter wird wegen eines versteckten Abhörgeräts festgenommen
articles.preview: Ein OpenAI-Mitarbeiter ist festgenommen worden, weil er ein Abhörgerät in einem Konferenzraum versteckt haben soll. Laut OpenAI gibt es bisher keine Hinweise, dass er auf Modelle, Quellcode oder Kundendaten zugegriffen hat.

summary.t: Das Gerät steckte versteckt im USB-Anschluss eines Fernsehers, ein zweites fand sich in einer Tasche des Mannes. Laut Justizministerium wurden über den Chatbot-Account seiner Ehefrau Fragen zu Aufnahmegeräten gestellt. Ihm drohen bis zu fünf Jahre Haft, und die US-Regierung nutzt den Fall als Beleg für die Bedeutung des KI-Wettlaufs.

articles.title: Teaching students to think and learn through questions
articles.preview: For Teachers' Day, OpenAI has released its free AI for Educators course in Brazilian Portuguese. It also highlights ChatGPT's Study Mode, which teaches through questions instead of handing out answers.

summary.t: Study Mode works through a topic step by step with questions, hints and checks, and was developed with teachers and education researchers. OpenAI suggests teachers test it on subjects they know well, for example letting students explore a topic and then write their own explanation without the chat in front of them.

articles.title: The EU’s next chapter in AI is agentic
articles.preview: A new OpenAI study finds that agentic AI is spreading quickly in European companies: weekly users of Codex and ChatGPT Work in small and mid-sized EU firms have grown more than eightfold since May. Leading EU companies still use AI far less intensively than the global front-runners.

summary.t: Among enterprise customers, agents already account for more than half of all AI output in the EU sample, but the share ranges from 22 percent in Slovenia to 85 percent in Lithuania. The most intensive EU users produce four times as much as typical firms, yet only half as much as top companies elsewhere, and EU firms make up just a tenth of the global leaders. OpenAI argues companies need help moving past experiments, along with skills training and more affordable access.

articles.title: Marktbericht: TSMC gibt sich keine Blöße
articles.preview: TSMC hat erneut einen Rekordgewinn von umgerechnet rund 21 Milliarden Euro im Quartal gemeldet und bestätigt sein Investitionsziel von 64 Milliarden Dollar. Trotzdem fallen Tech-Aktien, weil Anleger steigende Zinsen fürchten.

summary.t: Für das laufende Quartal erwartet TSMC eine weitere Beschleunigung des Wachstums, für das Gesamtjahr ein Umsatzplus von 44 Prozent. Analysten warnen dennoch, dass teuer finanzierte Rechenzentren außerhalb der großen Cloud-Konzerne zur Massenware werden könnten. In Südkorea brach der Leitindex um rund neun Prozent ein, und im DAX verloren Infineon und Siemens Energy am stärksten.

articles.title: Marktbericht: DAX vom Tech-Ausverkauf kaum betroffen
articles.preview: Der DAX hat den weltweiten Tech-Ausverkauf weitgehend abgeschüttelt und leicht im Plus bei 25.382 Punkten geschlossen. Große KI-Werte sind im deutschen Leitindex kaum vertreten.

summary.t: Hierzulande bewegen eher hohe Ölpreise und die Schulden von Frankreich und Italien die Anleger. In den USA schüren die Inflation von 3,7 Prozent und unerwartet hohe Erzeugerpreise die Angst vor einer weiteren Zinserhöhung der Fed, die Ende Oktober tagt. Dabei sprechen die Zahlen der Branche, etwa von ASML und TSMC, weiter für einen starken KI-Boom.

articles.title: Marktbericht: Europa wertvollster Konzern ASML macht KI-Boom möglich
articles.preview: Der Chipausrüster ASML hat seinen Quartalsgewinn auf knapp fünf Milliarden Euro gesteigert und ist mit über 600 Milliarden Euro Börsenwert Europas wertvollstes Unternehmen. Einige Kunden wollen schon Maschinen für 2029 und 2030 bestellen.

summary.t: Nur ASML baut die Lithografiemaschinen, mit denen die modernsten KI-Chips gefertigt werden, zu den Kunden zählen TSMC, Samsung und Intel. Der Umsatz stieg im Quartal auf knapp 11,7 Milliarden Euro, und für 2027 und 2028 reicht die geplante Kapazität nicht für alle Bestellungen. Ein Fondsmanager sieht kein Ende des Investitionszyklus, warnt aber, dass steigende Zinsen den schuldenfinanzierten Ausbau gefährden könnten.
